column1: What is Ehrlich's foundational axiom in receptor pharmacology ('corpora non agunt nisi fixata')?
column2: Substances do not act unless they are bound — a drug must bind a receptor/enzyme/channel/transporter in a concentration-dependent, saturable manner to exert a classical pharmacological effect.

column1: Differentiate affinity from efficacy in drug-receptor pharmacology.
column2: Affinity is how tightly a drug binds its receptor (quantified by Kd, the concentration producing 50% occupancy); efficacy is the magnitude of functional response generated per receptor bound.

column1: How do agonists, antagonists, and inverse agonists differ mechanistically in terms of receptor conformational states?
column2: Agonists stabilize the active conformation and increase its frequency; antagonists bind without favoring either state, blocking endogenous ligand access; inverse agonists shift equilibrium toward the inactive conformation, suppressing constitutive activity.

column1: What does bioavailability (F) equal for an IV-administered drug, and why?
column2: F = 1 (100%), because IV administration bypasses all absorption barriers and delivers drug directly into systemic circulation, avoiding first-pass metabolism.

column1: What does Volume of Distribution (Vd) actually represent?
column2: A proportionality constant relating total drug amount in the body to measured plasma concentration — not an actual physiological volume, but an apparent distribution volume.

column1: Which adrenergic receptor mediates vasoconstriction on vascular smooth muscle, and which mediates increased heart rate/contractility?
column2: Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle cause vasoconstriction; Beta-1 receptors on the SA node/ventricular myocardium mediate increased chronotropy, inotropy, and dromotropy.

column1: Why do M2 and M3 muscarinic receptors produce opposite cardiovascular effects despite both responding to acetylcholine?
column2: M2 (SA/AV node) hyperpolarizes pacemaker cells via G-protein-coupled inward rectifier K+ channels, slowing heart rate; M3 (vascular endothelium) stimulates eNOS, releasing NO that activates guanylyl cyclase in smooth muscle, causing vasodilation.

column1: What physicochemical properties allow a drug to cross the blood-brain barrier reliably?
column2: LogP between 1.5–2.5 and molecular weight below 400–500 Daltons, allowing penetration of endothelial tight junctions and astrocytic endfeet.

column1: Why does zolpidem cause less next-day sedation/hangover compared to non-selective benzodiazepines?
column2: Zolpidem is α1-subunit selective at the GABA-A receptor, producing hypnotic effects while sparing the α2/3 subunits responsible for anxiolysis and some sedation side effects.

column1: How is selective toxicity quantified in antimicrobial pharmacology, and give an example of high vs. low therapeutic index.
column2: Via the therapeutic index (TD50/ED50). Penicillin (targets bacterial cell wall absent in humans) has a large therapeutic index; amphotericin B (targets fungal ergosterol, similar to host cholesterol) has a narrow one.

column1: Contrast time-dependent vs. concentration-dependent antimicrobial killing, with the PK/PD target for each.
column2: Time-dependent agents (beta-lactams, macrolides) kill based on duration free drug exceeds MIC (fT>MIC, target 40–60% of dosing interval). Concentration-dependent agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) kill based on peak concentration relative to MIC (Cmax/MIC) and AUC/MIC, favoring high peak/extended intervals.

column1: State Paracelsus's core toxicological principle and its implication for therapeutic index interpretation.
column2: 'The dose makes the poison' — any compound therapeutic at one dose can be toxic at a higher dose; therapeutic index (TD50/ED50 or LD50/ED50) quantifies this safety margin, with narrow-index drugs (digoxin, warfarin, lithium) requiring strict therapeutic drug monitoring.
